analysis.one_liner: Let Medicare beneficiaries buy prescription drugs at Federal Supply Schedule prices.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: Rep. Bart Stupak proposed that every person eligible for Medicare could buy prescription drugs at Federal Supply Schedule prices — the discounted rates the federal government already pays for drugs it buys through the Veterans Administration and other agencies. The bill would have effectively let tens of millions of seniors and disabled beneficiaries tap into the government's bulk-buying power, paying lower prices at the pharmacy instead of retail prices. It was referred to two House committees and a subcommittee, where it sat until Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries — roughly 40 million seniors and disabled Americans at the time — would pay the government's discounted prices instead of retail, potentially saving hundreds of dollars a year per person on prescriptions.

how_it_helps.text: The bill declares that anyone entitled to Medicare part A or enrolled in part B is eligible to obtain prescription drugs at Federal Supply Schedule prices [S3].

The Federal Supply Schedule is the discounted price list the federal government already negotiates for drugs it purchases for programs like the Veterans Administration; extending it to Medicare would give beneficiaries access to those lower prices [S2].
The CRS summary confirms the purpose: making all Medicare beneficiaries eligible for drugs at those specified federal prices [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical manufacturers would receive lower net prices on a large share of the U.S. prescription market, and pharmacies would dispense at reduced reimbursement rates.

drawbacks.text: The bill is one sentence long. It states eligibility but contains no mechanism, no enforcement detail, and no funding — leaving open how pharmacies would be paid, how the discount would be administered, and what legal authority it rests on [S3].

The Federal Supply Schedule prices reflect what the government pays for its own purchases; applying them directly to individual retail prescriptions could reduce pharmacy reimbursement significantly, which pharmacies would argue threatens their viability, especially small independent drugstores [S3].
Drug manufacturers could absorb lower government prices by raising prices for everyone else, an effect the bill does not address.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to Medicare beneficiaries would have been large and immediate — access to the same discounted prices the government pays for its own drug purchases. The main costs fall on drug makers and, potentially, pharmacies. The bill's fatal weakness is design: it is a single substantive sentence with no administrative machinery, so even sympathetic committee members had no workable framework to advance. A better-drawn version could have delivered the same savings with less collateral damage to pharmacies.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees and then a subcommittee, and no committee ever acted on it before Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. Bart Stupak (D-MI) introduced the bill on July 17, 2002 [S1].
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, the two panels with jurisdiction over Medicare and drugs [S5].
On July 29, 2002, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health in Energy and Commerce; no further action was taken for the rest of the Congress [S5].
The 107th Congress ended January 3, 2003, so the bill expired in subcommittee without a hearing, markup, or vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical manufacturers were better off: nothing constrained what Medicare beneficiaries pay for prescriptions, and the bill's approach of extending federal discount prices died without ever being debated.

for.name: Rep. Bart Stupak
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to extend Federal Supply Schedule drug prices to all Medicare beneficiaries.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill, referred it to the Subcommittee on Health, and never scheduled a hearing or markup.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill for matters within its jurisdiction and took no action.

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers
against.role: Industry whose prices the bill would have cut
against.what_they_did: The industry strongly opposed letting Medicare beneficiaries buy at federal discount prices during this period, as it would have reduced revenues across its largest market.

sides.party_line_note: No votes or hearings occurred, and the bill attracted no cosponsors from either party, so the partisan divide never surfaced in the record.

industries.note: Extending Federal Supply Schedule prices to all Medicare beneficiaries would have cut the prices drug companies charge tens of millions of their largest customers. The industry's interest in blocking this ran directly against beneficiaries' savings.

Pharmacies would have been reimbursed at lower federal prices on a huge volume of prescriptions. The bill contained no transition or payment mechanism, so the hit to pharmacy margins — particularly small independents — was a real concern.
